**Answer: 6**

I did not complete a rigorous proof. This answer rests on a partial game analysis, not a verified strategy or a full second-player defense.

**Setup.** The nine 3×3 subsquares are indexed S(i,j) for i,j ∈ {1,2,3}, where S(i,j) covers rows i..i+2 and columns j..j+2. The first player places 13 ones and the second places 12 zeros. Any two subsquares overlap, and the center cell (3,3) lies in all nine.

**Why 5 is not easy for the second player.** A symmetry strategy fails. Central symmetry (r,c)↔(6−r,6−c) lets the first player take all eight non-center cells of a corner square. Reflection symmetry fails on the odd central column and on the squares that split across pairs.

**Why 6 looks achievable for the first player.** Let the second player aim to keep every square at no more than five ones, i.e. at least four zeros, by answering threats. The first player can repeatedly create double threats. In one line I checked, the first player takes the center, then makes threats on several squares at once. The second player can patch each double threat with a single zero, but eventually the first player finds a move that raises two squares to a deficit that cannot be patched with one cell. One square then has a common-empty structure that lets the first player secure six ones in it. This is a single line of play, not a full case analysis, and a better second-player defense may exist.

ANSWER: 6
